compiler_and_flags: J2CL Java-to-Wasm output optimized with Binaryen wasm-opt (Binaryen's README lists J2CL/J2Wasm as a wasm-opt user); exact flags not seen
name: J2CL WasmGC backend (Google Sheets calculation worker port)
baseline: The same Java code transpiled by J2CL to Closure-compiled JavaScript, running in V8 (Chrome)
workload: Google Sheets spreadsheet calculation worker, written in Java, built once as JavaScript through J2CL and once as WasmGC, calculation time measured in Chrome by the Sheets team.
claimed_speedup: WasmGC build about 2x faster calculation than the JavaScript build; speculative inlining plus devirtualization alone cut Chrome calculation time by about 40% (snippet only, taken from localized copies of the web.dev case study).
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; the Wasm output runs in production in Google Sheets
tradeoffs: Output needs a browser with WasmGC (Chrome 119 or later and other current engines) and a Binaryen optimization step. Java source is required, so this only helps code already written in Java. JS interop and browser-native APIs still cross the Wasm boundary.
caveats: Snippet only: the case-study page itself could not be fetched here (host not resolvable), so the numbers come from WebSearch snippets of localized copies and the page URL was not opened. First-party Google claim on the proprietary Sheets calculation engine, not reproducible from the repo; no hardware stated. The same case study reports that moving regex from a WasmGC-compiled re2j to Chrome's native RegExp made regex operations nearly 100x faster, and that the earlier JavaScript build was about 3x slower than the Java build on the server, so the 2x gain recovers only part of that gap. The repo has a benchmarking/ folder (`j2 bench` runs Closure, Wasm and JVM targets, example Box2dBenchmark under benchmarks/octane) but no published results were seen.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Wasm GC compiled language faster than JavaScript benchmark blog wasm_of_ocaml OR Kotlin/Wasm OR J2CL OR Dart wasm OR Scala.js wasm' surfaced the web.dev Google Sheets WasmGC case study; repo opened at github.com/google/j2cl and github.com/google/j2cl/tree/master/benchmarking.

compiler_and_flags: Rust compiled to wasm32 for the wasm-mappings crate; exact flags not seen
name: source-map (Rust-to-WebAssembly mappings parser in mozilla/source-map 0.7 and later)
language: Rust (compiled to WebAssembly) with a JavaScript API
baseline: The earlier pure-JavaScript source-map 0.6 mappings parser and consumer running in the browser JS engines
workload: Parsing a source map's mappings string and querying original/generated positions on real-world source maps, as reported in Mozilla's 'Oxidizing Source Maps with Rust and WebAssembly' post.
claimed_speedup: Up to 5.89x faster than the JavaScript implementation on realistic benchmarks over real-world source maps, with lower relative standard deviation (snippet only).
stars_or_usage: 3.7k stars; widely used by JS tooling and browser devtools
tradeoffs: The consumer API became asynchronous: SourceMapConsumer.initialize must be given the URL or bytes of lib/mappings.wasm, and consumers must call destroy() to free manually managed wasm memory. Bundlers and browsers need the extra wasm file.
caveats: Snippet only: the Mozilla Hacks post could not be fetched here (host not resolvable), so the 5.89x figure comes from WebSearch snippets and the page URL was not opened. Numbers date from January 2018 and compare against the 2018 JavaScript implementation; engines have changed since. 'Up to' is the best case. Repo has a browser benchmark harness (bench/README.md and bench/bench.html) but no committed results, compiler flags or CPU model. The same repo is also surfaced by wave 13 wasmlib searches.
found_via: WebSearch: 'rewrote JavaScript library in Rust WebAssembly benchmark faster than JS engineering blog' surfaced the Mozilla Hacks post; repo opened at github.com/mozilla/source-map and its raw README, package.json, bench/README.md and wasm-mappings files.

compiler_and_flags: wasm_of_ocaml with Binaryen 119 or later; flags not seen
name: wasm_of_ocaml (OCaml to WebAssembly GC compiler in ocsigen/js_of_ocaml)
baseline: js_of_ocaml (OCaml bytecode to JavaScript) output running in Node.js / V8
workload: OCaml programs compiled once by wasm_of_ocaml and once by js_of_ocaml, timed in Node.js. The repo's benchmarks/ directory (CamlBoy, Fiat Crypto, ocamlc, partial-render-table and others, report-wasm-cb.config with js_of_ocaml on node as the reference) is the harness; which workloads the quoted figure covers was not confirmed.
claimed_speedup: Early benchmarks suggested compiled programs typically run around 10-20% faster than the js_of_ocaml equivalent (preliminary figure from a late-2023 OCaml forum update, snippet only).
tradeoffs: Generated code needs the Wasm GC, tail-call and exception-handling extensions (Chrome 119, Node.js 22, Firefox 122, Safari 18.2 or newer) and a system Binaryen. OCaml 5 effects are slower with --effects=jspi and need CPS or stack switching on other engines.
caveats: Snippet only: the forum post could not be fetched here (host not resolvable) and the URL was not opened; the 10-20% figure is a 2023 preliminary result and later versions are not quantified. A newer ocaml.org post (April 2026) also could not be opened. The repo harness records timings but its README states no CPU model, Node.js version or flags (run.config is tuned per machine). Licence: dune-project declares GPL-2.0-or-later and LGPL-2.1-or-later with the OCaml linking exception; the LICENSE file describes LGPL 2.1 with that exception for the compiler and library.
found_via: WebSearch: 'wasm_of_ocaml OR TeaVM OR Hoot Scheme WebAssembly GC backend benchmark faster than JavaScript output js_of_ocaml blog' surfaced the ocaml-wasm organisation update on discuss.ocaml.org; repo opened at github.com/ocsigen/js_of_ocaml, its README_wasm_of_ocaml.md, CHANGES.md and benchmarks/ directory.

compiler_and_flags: TypeScript 5 build run under Node.js via `npm run bench`; Node.js version and flags not stated
name: LUME Kiwi (@lume/kiwi, TypeScript Cassowary constraint solver)
workload: Benchmark.js ops/sec for creating constraint problems (creation benchmark) and for solving them (solving benchmark), Kiwi against Cassowary.js in Node.js; the README says an AssemblyScript/WebAssembly build is planned ('Soon it will be compiled to WebAssembly').
claimed_speedup: Creation: Cassowary.js 2,597 ops/sec vs kiwi 26,243 ops/sec (about 10.11x faster, as printed). Solving: 260,002 vs 595,455 ops/sec (about 2.29x faster, as printed).
tradeoffs: Pure TypeScript/JavaScript, no wasm delivered yet; API differs from Cassowary.js (a 'new API' variant is also benchmarked at 20,840 ops/sec for creation).
caveats: The numbers are a 'sample result output' in the README with no hardware, Node.js version or date. First-party benchmark with partial methodology. The category fit is weak: the speed-up is a TypeScript rewrite over another JS library, not WebAssembly; the AssemblyScript build is only announced. The LICENSE file URL returned 404, licence taken from package.json.
